etfs.brief: Buying the whole S&P 500 through VOO returned 16.9% over the past year, before dividends, for a fee of 0.03% a year — about $3 annually on every $10,000 invested. Fees across this list run from 0.03% to 0.20%. That gap sounds trivial and is not: it is deducted every year, on the whole balance, whether the fund rises or falls. This is the benchmark the rest of the dashboard has to beat. Picking individual companies only makes sense if it does better than simply buying the index, after the effort and the mistakes — and today the screen finds 4 of 23 tracked companies trading below their estimated value. Buffett's own instruction for his estate was 90% in a low-cost S&P 500 fund and 10% in short-term government bonds. He has been explicit that most people, including his own family, should not try to pick stocks at all.

glossary.group: The idea behind the whole dashboard
glossary.blurb: Warren Buffett buys pieces of businesses, not tickets on share prices. Everything here follows from that.

terms.definition: A slice of ownership in a real company. Owning one share of a company with a million shares means you own a millionth of its profits, its buildings and its debts. The price on the screen is just what somebody will pay you for that slice today.
Working out what a business is genuinely worth, then buying only if the market is asking less than that. The opposite is guessing which way the price will move next.

What the business is actually worth, based on the cash it will produce for its owners over its life. Nobody can know it exactly; every figure on this dashboard is an estimate with its assumptions shown.

Only buying at a decent discount to your estimate, because your estimate might be wrong. If you think a business is worth $100 a share and you insist on paying under $70, you can be 30% too optimistic and still not lose money.

Whatever stops competitors from stealing a company's profits: a brand people insist on, costs nobody can match, or the sheer hassle of switching away. Without one, high profits attract rivals until the profits are gone.
The set of businesses you actually understand well enough to judge. Buffett treats staying inside it as non-negotiable, and it is the one test no dashboard can run for you.

glossary.blurb: Companies must publish their finances. These are the numbers the dashboard pulls out of those filings.

terms.definition: All the money that came in from selling things, before any costs. Also called sales or the top line.
What is left after every cost, including tax. Also called profit, earnings, or the bottom line.

Cash a company pays out to its shareholders, usually quarterly. It is the other half of what you earn from a share, alongside the price moving. Profit either gets paid out this way or kept and reinvested.
What the owners would in theory have left if the company sold everything and paid off all its debts. It comes from the accounts, not the stock market.

Profit divided by that owners' stake: how much the company earns on the money shareholders have left in it. Buffett looks for 15% or more, held for years. A company earning $15 on every $100 of owners' money is a far better machine than one earning $3.

The same idea, but counting borrowed money too. The dashboard switches to this when a company has bought back so much of its own stock that its book equity is near zero and ROE stops meaning anything.
Of every $100 of sales, how much survives after the direct cost of making the product. A steady gross margin over ten years is the best outside evidence that a moat is real.
Money spent on physical things the business needs: factories, machines, shops, servers. It is real cash leaving the company even though it is not counted as a cost in the profit line straight away.
The accountant's way of spreading the cost of equipment over the years it is used, rather than all at once. It is a bookkeeping entry, not cash going out of the door this year.

Buffett's own measure, and the one this dashboard values companies on: profit, plus bookkeeping charges like depreciation that did not really cost cash, minus the capital spending genuinely needed to keep the business where it is. It answers what an owner could actually take out each year without the business shrinking.
A close cousin: the cash generated by operations minus all capital spending, including spending on growth.

An admission that something the company owns is worth less than the books said, often a business it overpaid for. It hits reported profit hard but no cash moves, which is why the dashboard adds it back.
How many slices the company is divided into. It matters enormously: the same business split into twice as many shares means each share is worth half as much.
A company using its cash to purchase its own shares and cancel them, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice. Good value when the shares are cheap, wasteful when they are expensive.

Profits the company kept and reinvested instead of paying out. Buffett's test is that every $1 kept should eventually create at least $1 of market value, or shareholders would have been better off with the cash.

glossary.group: Working out what a business is worth
glossary.blurb: How the dashboard turns those numbers into a price per share.

terms.definition: The method behind the estimate. Add up the cash the business should produce over the next ten years plus a value for everything after that, then shrink those future amounts to reflect that money later is worth less than money now.
The annual return you insist on for taking the risk, used to shrink those future amounts. Higher discount rate, lower value today. The dashboard defaults to 10% and lets you change it with a slider.

The lump that stands for everything the business earns beyond year ten. It is usually half or more of any DCF result, which is worth knowing: most of the 'value' rests on a guess about the distant future. Each company page shows what share it makes up.
How fast you assume the business grows forever after year ten. It has to be modest, because nothing grows faster than the whole economy indefinitely. The default here is 2.5%.
Profit divided by the price you pay, expressed as a percentage. It lets you compare a share directly with a savings account or a government bond.
Price divided by annual profit per share. A P/E of 25 means you are paying 25 years of current profit for the stake. Lower is cheaper, all else being equal, but all else rarely is.
The same calculation run on pessimistic, middling and optimistic growth assumptions, so you see a range rather than one falsely precise number.

glossary.blurb: Context for whether shares in general are cheap or dear right now.

terms.definition: A basket tracking many companies at once, used as shorthand for how a whole market is doing. The S&P 500 holds 500 large American firms; TA-125 holds the 125 largest in Tel Aviv.

Gross domestic product: the total value of everything a country produces in a year. It is the standard measure of how big an economy is, and it is the figure the stock market gets compared against just below.

The value of every listed company added together, divided by GDP. So a reading of 200% means the stock market is worth twice everything the country produces in a year. Buffett called it the best single measure of whether shares are expensive. Around 100% is historically normal; today's reading is far above that.

A Treasury is a loan to the American government, and its yield is what that loan pays you. It counts as the safest return available, so Buffett calls it gravity: every share has to beat it, or you should simply buy the bond instead. The 10-year Treasury is the one quoted on this page.
A gauge of how much turbulence traders expect in the next month. High means fear, low means calm — and calm markets are usually expensive ones.
The price of one share multiplied by the number of shares: what the market says the whole company is worth.

The trap of judging by the winners because the losers have quietly disappeared from the list. A table of the best-performing funds looks wonderful precisely because the failures are not in it. Any ranked list on this page, including the fund tables, has to be read with that in mind.

glossary.blurb: Buffett's advice to almost everyone is not to pick stocks at all, but to buy the whole market cheaply and leave it alone.

terms.definition: A pot of money from many people, invested together and run by a manager. You own a slice of the pot rather than the individual holdings.
A fund that simply buys everything in an index, in the same proportions, and makes no attempt to pick winners. Because nobody is being paid to choose, it is very cheap to run.
A fund you buy and sell on the stock exchange like a single share, rather than through the fund company. Most ETFs are index funds, and the two words are often used loosely to mean the same thing.

The percentage the fund takes each year, deducted automatically from the fund's value. It is the single most important number on this page: 0.03% costs $3 a year on $10,000, while 1% costs $100, every year, whether the fund rises or falls.

Price return counts only the change in price. Total return also counts the dividends paid along the way. The fund figures on this dashboard are price returns, so a fund paying income has done somewhat better than shown.

A fund that borrows in order to multiply the index's daily move, two or three times over. It multiplies losses just as faithfully, and among the Israeli funds listed here the leveraged category spans the widest range of outcomes by far.

glossary.blurb: A different discipline entirely. These say nothing about what a business is worth, and are on the dashboard only for timing a purchase you have already decided on.

terms.definition: The average closing price over the last 50 or 200 days, which smooths out the daily noise. Price above the long average is conventionally read as an uptrend.
A 0-100 score of how hard a share has been bought or sold lately. Above 70 is called overbought, below 30 oversold. It is a crowd-mood reading, not a statement about the business.
How much the price typically moves in a day. Useful for deciding how large a position you can hold without a normal wobble forcing you to sell.
The highest and lowest the price has been in the past year. A share near its low is not automatically cheap, but it is a reasonable place to start looking.

glossary.blurb: American companies must file their accounts publicly. This dashboard reads those filings directly rather than trusting a summary.

terms.definition: The US Securities and Exchange Commission, the regulator that requires listed companies to publish their finances honestly and on time.
The SEC's free public archive where all those filings live.
The annual report: a company's full audited accounts for the year, plus a discussion of its risks and business.
The lighter quarterly version, filed three times a year.
A one-off announcement of something significant between reports, such as an acquisition or a chief executive leaving.
A quarterly list every large investment manager must file showing what US shares they own. This is how the dashboard knows what Berkshire Hathaway holds — though it arrives up to 45 days late.
The company Buffett has run since 1965, and the vehicle through which he invests.
The machine-readable tagging inside modern filings that lets software read a balance sheet without a human retyping it.

glossary.blurb: Israeli terms used on the Israel tab. These are funds rather than operating companies, so none of the Buffett tests above apply to them.

terms.definition: A fund holding very short-term, very safe debt. The closest thing to cash that still pays interest: no lock-up, minimal risk, and a yield that follows the Bank of Israel's rate. Useful as the benchmark anything riskier has to beat.

terms.term: Hedge fund in trust (קרן גידור בנאמנות)
terms.definition: An Israeli fund allowed to use strategies ordinary funds cannot, such as betting that a share will fall. Sold to the public in a regulated wrapper, but with higher fees and much wider outcomes.
The percentage the manager charges every year, whether or not they make you money. On a money-market fund it matters enormously, because it comes straight out of a small return.
An extra cut of the profits, typically 20% among the Israeli hedge funds listed here. It means the return you read in the table is not the return that reaches your pocket.
An Israeli labelling rule. The digit is how much can be in shares (0 = none, 6 = up to 200%), and the letter is foreign-currency exposure (A = none, F = up to 200%). So 5E means a lot of both.
A fund that both owns shares it expects to rise and bets against shares it expects to fall. It can profit in a falling market, and can also lose in a rising one.
The main Tel Aviv indices: the 125 largest listed Israeli companies, and the 35 largest within them.
The family of Tel Aviv indices tracking corporate bonds rather than shares.

The interest rate Israel's central bank sets, which is the anchor for what every safe shekel investment pays. When it rises, money-market funds pay more within weeks; when it falls, they pay less. It is the Israeli equivalent of the Treasury yield as a hurdle.
How many shekels one US dollar buys. It matters because the American companies on the other tabs are priced in dollars, so a stronger shekel quietly reduces their value to you.

principle.title: Beware the institutional imperative
principle.body: Organisations imitate their peers, resist changing direction, and find justifications for whatever leadership already wants to do. Buffett names this tendency as a major destroyer of capital and looks for managers who visibly resist it.

disclaimer: This dashboard reports public filings and applies published screening criteria. It is not investment advice, does not know your circumstances, and makes no recommendation to buy or sell anything. Every estimate here depends on assumptions that are shown alongside it and that you should judge for yourself.
